fact: The four basic steps for setting up an aquarium are preparing the substrate and decorations, conditioning the water, ensuring proper glass sealing, and understanding the fish species to be stocked
Setup step, substrate and decorations: use gravel, sand or a planted substrate and include decorations for fish to hide and explore
Setup step, condition the water: dechlorinate tap water and ensure proper temperature before adding fish
Setup step, glass sealing: make sure the glass is of the required thickness and properly sealed to avoid leakage of water
Setup step, know your fish species: do not stock two types of fish that cannot cohabit, where one is aggressive to the other
Daily maintenance is to feed small amounts 1 to 2 times a day and to observe the fish for signs of stress, disease or unusual behaviour
Overfeeding and the accumulation of uneaten feed in a fish tank or pond leads to water pollution
Weekly maintenance is a partial water change replacing 20 to 30 per cent of the water to remove toxins, checking water parameters, and cleaning the glass and decorations
Regular water changes are recommended for maintaining good water quality in an aquarium
The weekly parameter check tests for pH, ammonia, nitrites and nitrates
The glass and decorations are cleaned with an algae scraper, salt-sterilised foam or a magnetic cleaner to remove algae buildup
Monthly maintenance is filter maintenance, rinsing filter media in tank water and not tap water to preserve beneficial bacteria, and inspecting heaters, filters, pumps and lights
Long-term care is monitoring fish health by quarantining new fish before adding them to the main tank, and trimming or replacing live plants
Poor water quality causes stress and reduced immunity, toxicity issues where high ammonia poisons fish, and parasite and bacterial infections such as Aeromonas
Fish under stress eat less and grow more slowly, increasing production time and costs, and severe hypoxia can cause sudden fish deaths and huge financial losses
Poor water quality also produces poor skin and fin conditions that make fish less marketable, and uncontrolled algae growth
Fish talk by expressing themselves through their behavioural patterns, so understanding their body language is essential to rearing them to marketable size
The four fish behaviour categories taught are inability to eat, hungry fishes, slow movement and stress
Inability to eat, pattern: slow movement, inactivity, gasping for air at the surface or breathing rapidly, hanging motionless in one spot, and rejecting feed intake
Inability to eat, cause: polluted water quality or illness and infection, along with unbalanced feed, low or high temperature, stress and overfeeding

Inability to eat, remedy: drain out dirty water and refill with fresh clean water, treat sick fishes, allow the fish to rest if overfed, feed at the right time with well-balanced feed, and test and correct water parameters
Hungry fishes, pattern: swimming towards you, becoming more active, begging at the surface with open mouths, gathering at the usual feeding spot, and jumping or lunging at food as soon as it appears
Hungry fishes, cause: low-quality fish feed, insufficient feed intake, and competition for food where dominant fish eat more while others stay hungry
Hungry fishes, remedy: feed the fish to satiation to avoid cannibalism
Sorting and grading of fish according to their sizes allows uniform distribution of fish feed and ultimate consumption
Hungry fishes, further remedies: maintain a consistent feeding schedule and control competition by spreading feed across the tank or using sinking pellets for bottom feeders
Slow movement, pattern: staying near the bottom, reduced response to stimuli, sluggish or disoriented swimming, gasping near the surface, fins folded close to the body, and avoiding open spaces
Slow movement, cause: poor water quality, low oxygen levels, temperature issues, disease or parasites such as Ich and fin rot, nutritional deficiency, stress from overcrowding, and overfeeding
Slow movement, remedy: increase aeration using air stones, filters, air pumps and live plants

Slow movement, further remedies: test and improve water parameters, maintain proper temperature, treat with appropriate medication and quarantine sick fish, provide high-quality balanced food, ensure enough space, and avoid overfeeding
Stress in fish is a physiological response to unfavourable environmental conditions that weakens the immune system, making fish more susceptible to diseases and even death
Stress, pattern: clamped fins held close to the body, faded body colour and avoiding open areas to hide, along with erratic swimming, refusing food and rapid breathing
Stress, cause: sudden temperature fluctuations, which the text calls shock, and improper acclimatisation to new water conditions

Stress, further causes: poor water quality, insufficient oxygen, overcrowding and bullying from bigger aggressive fish, nutritional deficiencies, overfeeding, frequent netting or moving between tanks, and loud noises or vibrations

Stress, remedy: maintain water quality, keep a stable temperature with a heater or chiller, increase oxygenation, keep compatible sizes with enough space, provide housing or plant trees over fishponds, provide quality balanced feed, limit disturbances, and acclimate new fish properly
Behaviour is studied because changes in swimming patterns, feeding behaviour or respiration indicate stress or disease, and fish gasping at the surface may signal low oxygen levels
Observing feeding response prevents overfeeding or underfeeding, and efficient feeding reduces waste, improves growth rates and minimises water pollution
Underfeeding and overfeeding fish are not good practices for fish growth and health
Overcrowding causes stress, competition for food and increased disease risk, and some species exhibit aggressive or cannibalistic behaviour especially when food is scarce
An aquarium is described as a beauty to behold, with air bubbles from the air pump, colourful ornamental fish and decorations, requiring consistent care and attention
